name: The Café Wall Illusion
statement: Rows of offset dark and light tiles make the perfectly straight lines between them look sloped.
statementAccent: make the perfectly straight lines between them look sloped
meaning: The café wall illusion is a geometrical-optical illusion in which the parallel straight horizontal lines dividing rows of tiles appear to be sloped, converging and diverging in wedge shapes, when they are in fact perfectly parallel. The figure consists of staggered rows of alternating dark and light rectangular tiles, each row shifted horizontally relative to those above and below, with the rows separated by thin lines of grey mortar whose brightness is intermediate between the dark and light tiles. The offset tiles and the grey mortar together create the compelling impression that the horizontal mortar lines tilt. The illusion was described and named by Richard Gregory and Priscilla Heard, who published on it in 1979 after a member of Gregory's laboratory noticed it on the tiled wall of a café in Bristol, England. It is a variant of earlier illusions, including the Münsterberg illusion, and a classic in vision science.
mechanism: The illusion arises from the way the visual system processes luminance contrasts at the borders between the tiles and the mortar. At each tile edge, small local interactions between the adjacent dark and light regions produce tiny cues to tilt, and when these are combined along a row of offset tiles, they add up to a perceived slope of the horizontal mortar line, alternating into wedges. The grey mortar of intermediate brightness is essential: the illusion is strongest when the mortar is a thin line whose luminance sits near the midpoint between the dark and light tiles, and it disappears when the two tile colours are of equal brightness or when the mortar is removed. Gregory and Heard proposed a border-locking account, involving how the visual system detects and registers edges, and the effect also draws on brightness or irradiation phenomena at the tile borders. The exact mechanism is debated and thought to involve interactions among orientation-sensitive neurons in the visual cortex, since a residual illusion persists even when simple optical explanations are removed.

examples.text: The illusion is named for a tiled wall at a Bristol café, where offset rows of light and dark tiles made the straight mortar lines look wedge-shaped.
The thin grey mortar line, intermediate in brightness between the tiles, is crucial; without it, or with equal-brightness tiles, the illusion vanishes.
The offset of successive rows makes the parallel horizontal lines appear to tilt in alternating directions, forming a series of wedges.

variants.name: Border locking
variants.text: Gregory and Heard's proposed mechanism, in which the visual system's registration of tile-mortar borders produces the perceived tilt.

variants.name: The Munsterberg antecedent
variants.text: The earlier shifted-chessboard illusion described by Hugo Munsterberg, of which the café wall is a variant.

whyItMatters: The café wall illusion is a classic and much-studied illusion in vision science, valued for what it reveals about how the visual system processes edges, luminance contrast, and orientation. By making perfectly parallel lines appear sloped, it demonstrates that the perception of geometry is not a direct readout of the physical image but is constructed by neural processes that can be systematically fooled by contrast at borders. Its dependence on the intermediate-brightness mortar makes it a clean test case for theories of edge detection and brightness processing, and its resistance to full explanation has kept it a productive puzzle for researchers studying cortical orientation processing. As a vivid, memorable illusion that anyone can see and that arose from a real tiled wall, it is both a staple teaching example and a continuing subject of research into how the brain builds our perception of lines, edges, and shape.

working.text: stagger rows of alternating dark and light tiles so each row is shifted relative to its neighbours.
separate the rows with thin grey mortar lines of brightness midway between the dark and light tiles.
observe the parallel mortar lines appear to tilt into wedges, produced by contrast interactions at the tile borders.

limits: The café wall illusion depends on specific conditions: the tiles must be offset, and the mortar must be a thin line of intermediate brightness between the dark and light tiles, without which the illusion weakens or disappears. Its strength varies with tile size, contrast, mortar width, and viewing distance. The exact mechanism remains debated; while border-locking and brightness effects at the tile edges are widely invoked, the illusion is thought to involve cortical orientation processing that is not fully understood, and a residual component persists even when simple optical factors are controlled. Sources also differ slightly on the precise date the illusion was named. So the café wall illusion reliably demonstrates that contrast at borders can distort perceived orientation, while the complete account of why remains an open question in vision science.
misreadings: The lines really are parallel; the illusion is that they look sloped, so anyone measuring them finds no actual tilt. The effect is not merely about the tiles being offset; the intermediate-brightness grey mortar is essential, and removing it or using equal-brightness tiles destroys the illusion. And its cause is not fully settled: border-locking and contrast effects are leading accounts, but the mechanism involves debated cortical processing, so treating the illusion as a simple optical trick with a known cause overstates how well it is understood.
origin: Described and named by Richard Gregory and Priscilla Heard in 1979, after the illusion was noticed on the tiled wall of a café in Bristol, England; it is a variant of the earlier Munsterberg illusion.
